Why is tap water wider at the nozzle and thinner further down?

If you look at your nozzle from the lower side, you'll see a metal mesh. When a certain amount of water goes through the mesh, it does so at a wider area than if there were no mesh (because it has to squeeze through). After that it is "drawn together" again by surface tension, producing a slightly thinner ray. As to "breaking apart into droplets", it does that when its speed gets high enough that the air resistance is greater than the surface tension, at which point the ray splits into something like droplets, which hold together better by surface tension. There are other factors coming into play, but these are some of the important ones.

As to "breaking apart into droplets", it does that when its speed gets high enough that the air resistance is greater than the surface tension, at which point the ray splits into something like droplets, which hold together better by surface tension.

Does this mean that if you were to turn on a tap in a vacuum that it would never turn into droplets, no matter how far the water fell?

/u/mixplate

Huh, god idea, never tried. I'd answer no - I think it would take longer for the ray to break, but the longer it falls, the more opportunity the water has to diverge. Also, note that falling things accelerate, so while the water in your tap only gets up to speeds of, say, 1m/s, water that's been falling for 1 second will be going at a speed of 10m/s, and the water that's been falling for 2 seconds - 20m/s. Since the water furthest down is falling so much faster than that at the top (assuming the tap is constantly pouring), that "stretches out" the ray in the vertical direction, which will sooner or later make droplets form, tho they ought to look a bit different (more like vertical beads I guess).

The volume of water that leaves the tap in a given unit of time is relatively constant. As that volume of water drops, it is accelerated by gravity. That same volume of water is stretched over a greater distance when it's moving faster.
